problem: How to handle replacement requests from owners of affected chips.
title: Intel limits Pentium replacements, then offers to replace every flawed chip
context: Intel's Pentium processor had a floating-point division flaw (the FDIV bug) that became public in late 1994.
decision_made: First replace chips only for users who showed a need, then, under pressure, offer to replace every flawed Pentium on request.
action_taken: Announced the full replacement offer on 20 December 1994 and booked a $475 million pretax charge in the fourth quarter.
observed_outcome: The restrictive approach angered buyers. After the full offer, few owners asked for replacement; one report said most people kept their chips and that Intel might reverse part of the charge.
lessons: Restricting remedies for a visible flaw can cost more in trust than an open offer would have cost in chips.
limitations: Breakdown of returns and scrapped chips is an outside estimate. Whether the charge was partly reversed was not confirmed.

claims.claim_text: Intel moved from questioning users before replacing chips to replacing all flawed Pentiums on request on 20 December 1994.
Intel took a $475 million pretax charge in Q4 1994 to cover replacement and write-off.
